analysis: Examined the head-side excerpts of fixtures/prompt-contract/v1/production_vectors.json (lines 52072-53487). The file is a public golden-vector test fixture holding synthetic cache-parity inputs, expected token IDs, prompt_contract_id and chain-hash block boundaries. The visible changes add an "additional_context": {"enable_thinking": false} member to template_input (e.g. lines 52354-52356, 53238-53240), reduce prompt_token_count and block boundaries (767 vs 803 previously), and change token IDs/chain hashes. The prompt_contract_id values and the chain hashes are expected to be consistent with the matching prompt-contract code, which is not supplied here. No secrets, credentials, real consumer data or keys are present; the content is public synthetic text ("Public synthetic cache-parity input"). The fixture changes no runtime authorization, attestation, encryption or App Attest behavior (TB-011, TB-002, A-016). Its only link to the threat model is the retained cache-sharing/TTFT threat T-041, which relies on chain-hash prefix keys for cache isolation; I could not verify from the supplied excerpts that the Swift or Go prompt-rendering and chain-hash code matches these vectors, nor that the cache key still scopes by scope_id. Those code changes are in other files and units. I did not see anything in these units that weakens scoping. The remaining integration question is whether the companion prompt-template and hashing code changes (enable_thinking default, contract id change) preserve cache-key domain separation, and whether the vectors are consumed by parity tests. No finding is supported by the supplied evidence.
